analysis.one_liner: Makes anyone who intentionally helps others commit copyright infringement legally liable as an infringer.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by the Senate Judiciary chairman and cosponsored by both party leaders, died in committee without a hearing or a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new rule to copyright law: anyone who intentionally aids, abets, or induces another person's copyright infringement could be sued as an infringer. Intent could be proven by showing that a product's business 'relies on infringement for its commercial viability.' The clear target was file-sharing software and networks that let users copy music and movies. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be the major record labels and movie studios, which would gain a new legal tool to sue not just people who copy music and movies, but the companies that make the software and devices used to copy them. Artists would get somewhat stronger backing for their copyrights, though the money flows through the labels and studios.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new basis for lawsuits: anyone who intentionally induces copyright infringement can be sued as an infringer, on top of existing rules for people who directly copy or who help indirectly.

Lets courts find intent from circumstances, including whether a product's business model depends on infringement, making it easier to sue file-sharing services rather than millions of individual users.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on technology companies that make general-purpose products — the bill's intent standard could sweep in software and devices used for both lawful and unlawful copying. Ordinary people would bear it as higher-risk, more conservative technology, more litigation, and less freedom to share and back up media. The bill expressly says it leaves existing secondary-liability rules alone, but the new inducement standard sits on top of them.

drawbacks.text: The 'intentionally induces' standard is broad: intent can be inferred from whether a business 'relies on infringement for its commercial viability,' which critics said could expose makers of general-purpose technologies — devices and software with legal uses — to lawsuits simply because some customers infringe.

Because liability is aimed at the toolmakers rather than individual copiers, the bill would have shifted a sprawling enforcement fight onto inventors, chilling new media technology in the name of protecting existing sales.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that existing law already covered companies that encourage infringement, and that the bill's added vagueness would mainly create litigation risk rather than new protection for working artists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered labels and studios a sharper legal weapon against file sharing, but at the price of a vague liability standard hanging over every maker of copy-capable technology. The cost — a chill on legitimate innovation and more legal risk for ordinary users of technology — outweighed the marginal protection it added for artists.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 22, 2004, by Senator Hatch along with six senators from both parties, including the Republican and Democratic floor leaders, and referred to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
It gathered 10 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 3 Republicans) but received no further committee action, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Technology companies and ordinary internet users came out ahead, because no new liability standard for making copy-capable products ever took effect. The record labels and studios, which had pushed for a new weapon against file-sharing, had to continue operating under the existing copyright rules.

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah and Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own Judiciary Committee, where it never received a hearing or markup.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont and ranking Democrat on the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined Hatch as an original sponsor of the bill.

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist and Sen. Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Majority Leader and Senate Minority Leader
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill top bipartisan leadership backing from both parties.

for.name: Recording Industry Association of America and Motion Picture Association
for.role: Trade groups for the major record labels and movie studios
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed the legislation as a way to shut down peer-to-peer file-sharing networks that they said were devastating music and movie sales.

against.name: Technology industry companies and trade associations
against.role: Software, computer, and consumer electronics makers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing the vague inducement standard could make them liable for infringement by users of their general-purpose products, and lobbied senators against advancing it.

against.name: Public interest and digital rights groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, warning it could chill technology innovation and restrict lawful uses of media by consumers.

sides.party_line_note: Support was split across both parties from the start: the bill was sponsored by the Republican Judiciary chairman and the top Democrat on the committee, with the Republican and Democratic Senate leaders among its original backers, and its 10 cosponsors split 7 Democrats to 3 Republicans; it died without a vote rather than along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have given labels a new lawsuit target — the makers of file-sharing software — instead of pursuing millions of individual users one at a time. The protection flows to labels and their artists through higher control over copying and distribution.
Studios would get the same new inducement liability to attack peer-to-peer movie sharing. Their interest in shutting down unauthorized copying runs against consumers' freedom to use and share media.

industries.industry: Software, consumer electronics, and internet companies
industries.note: A vague inducement standard could have exposed makers of general-purpose products — anything that can copy media — to infringement lawsuits, raising legal risk for inventors and their customers. Their interest in staying free of this liability ran alongside ordinary people's access to new technology.
